case_name: R. v. Westfair Foods Ltd. and Canada Safeway Ltd.
text:
Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench

Judicial Centre of Saskatoon

Citation: R. v. Westfair Foods Ltd. and
Canada Safeway Ltd.

Date: 1987-08-20

Docket: 56 A.D. 1986

Between:

Her Majesty The Queen (Appellant)

and

Westfair Foods Ltd. and Canada Safeway
Ltd. et al. (Respondents)

Wimmer, J.

Counsel:

Bill Davern, for the appellant;

R.G. Richards and B. Gale Welsh, for the
Attorney General for Saskatchewan;

L.F. Seiferling and Kathy M. Ring, for Westfair
Foods Ltd.;

D.C. Hodson, for Canada Safeway Ltd.

I

[
1
]

Wimmer, J.: In contention here is the constitutional validity of a
municipal bylaw governing the operating hours of retail stores and the
provincial legislation authorizing such bylaws .

[
2
]

Section 121 of the Urban Municipality Act, 1984 establishes a scheme for
the regulation of store hours. It specifies that all stores must remain closed
on weekdays between 6:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m. and on weekends between 10:00 p.m.
Saturday and 5:00 a.m. Monday. However, urban municipalities are empowered to
enact bylaws varying those hours in some respects. For example, urban
municipalities may permit stores to be open after 6:00 p.m. on certain days.
Also, the section exempts certain types of stores - such as convenience stores,
pharmacies, and garages - from its provisions, but urban municipalities are
authorized to classify those stores according to type, size, or location, and
to regulate their hours accordingly. The section also prescribes the penalties
to be imposed in the event of a breach of its provisions or of the provisions of
any bylaw enacted under its authority.

[
3
]

In March, 1986 the municipal council of the City of Saskatoon enacted
what is known as the
Store Hours Bylaw.
It is formally entitled
A
Bylaw of the City of Saskatoon to Provide for the Regulation of Store Hours.

It prohibits stores having a combined sale and display area of more than 1100
square meters from opening for business on Sundays, holidays, and after certain
hours on all other days. The same prohibition does not apply to smaller stores
where the' principal business is the sale of specified items of a kind usually
found in convenience stores, pharmacies, and garages. The provisions of the
bylaw are consistent with those authorized by s. 121 of the
Act.

[
4
]

Westfair Foods Ltd. and Canada Safeway Ltd. operate stores in the City
of Saskatoon. Each store has a combined sale or display area in excess of 1100
square meters. These stores have admittedly been kept open in defiance of the
bylaw. As a consequence, numerous charges were brought against both
corporations as well as against individual store managers.

[
5
]

When the charges came before the Provincial Court, and before any plea
was recorded, they were objected to on constitutional grounds. It was argued
for all of the respondents that both the bylaw and s. 121 of the
Act
are
invalid because they are inconsistent with certain provisions of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.
Specifically, it was argued that the bylaw
and s. 121 of the
Act
are inconsistent with the
Charter's

guaranteed freedom of conscience and religion (
s. 2(a)
) and its guaranteed
equality rights (
s. 15(1)
).

[
6
]

The Provincial Court Judge who decided the matter found no inconsistency
with
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
and none as between s. 121 of the
Act

and
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter.
However, he did find the bylaw to be
discriminatory and thus inconsistent with s. 15(1) and, being unable to
conclude that the discrimination was demonstrably justified within the meaning
of
s. 1
of the
Charter
, he dismissed all of the charges.

[
7
]

Each order of dismissal was appealed to this court. All of the appeals
were heard as one with the intention that they be disposed of in a single
opinion. The arguments advanced on appeal were similar to those considered and
ruled upon by the Provincial Court judge.

[
8
]

Having had the benefit of judgments from the Supreme Court of Canada and
the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan, which were not available to the
Provincial Court judge, I have reached a conclusion entirely opposite to his.

II

[
9
]

Section 2(a)
of the
Charter
guarantees to everyone the fundamental
freedom of conscience and religion. What is meant by freedom of religion has
been described by the Supreme Court of Canada in the following terms:

"The essence of the concept of freedom of religion is the
right to entertain such religious beliefs as a person chooses, the right to
declare religious beliefs openly and without fear of hindrance or reprisal, and
the right to manifest religious belief by worship and practice or by teaching
and dissemination. But the concept means more than that.

"Freedom can primarily be characterized by the absence of
coercion or constraint. If a person is compelled by the state or the will of
another to a course of action or inaction which he would not otherwise have
chosen, he is not acting of his own violition and he cannot be said to be truly
free. One of the major purposes of the
Charter
is to protect, within
reason, from compulsion or restraint. Coercion includes not only such blatant
forms of compulsion as direct commands to act or refrain from acting on pain of
sanction, coercion includes indirect forms of control which determine or limit
alternative courses of conduct available to others. Freedom in a broad sense
embraces both the absence of coercion and constraint, and the right to manifest
beliefs and practices. Freedom means that, subject to such limitations as are
necessary to protect public safety, order, health, or morals or the fundamental
rights and freedoms of others, no one is to be forced to act in a way contrary
to his beliefs or his conscience."

R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295; [1985] 3
W.W.R. 481; 58 N.R. 81; 60 A.R. 161; 18 C.C.C.(3d) 385; 18 D.L.R.(4th) 321, per
Dickson, J., at 336-337 (S.C.R.).

[
10
]

It is argued for the respondents that those provisions of the
Act

and the bylaw which compel stores to close on Sunday infringe this
constitutionally guaranteed freedom of religion. They do so, it is said,
because they coerce those retailers who observe some day other than Sunday as
their Sabbath (such as those of the Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist faiths) to
either close their stores one extra day each week or to transact business on
what is for them a religious holiday. Substantial support for the argument can
be marshalled from the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v.
Edwards Books and Art Ltd.
,
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713; 71 N.R. 161; 19 O.A.C.
239; 30 C.C.C.(3d) 385; 55 C.R.(3d) 193.

[
11
]

One of the questions posed in
R. v. Edwards Books
was whether the

Retail Business Holidays Act
of Ontario which prohibits the opening of
retail businesses on a holiday - a holiday by definition including Sunday -
infringes the fundamental freedom of religion guaranteed by s. 2(a). Although
it was held that the statute was enacted for the secular purpose of providing
common holidays for retail workers, the majority of the court found that it has
the effect of infringing the freedom of religion of those retailers who close
their stores on Saturdays for religious reasons. However, the majority also
found that the infringement is justifiable under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

[
12
]

The same purpose and effects test is to be applied in the present
appeals. The impugned legislation must first be examined to determine whether
its purpose alone is to hinder the exercise of any guaranteed right or freedom.
If it is found to have a valid purpose, then its effects must be examined to
determine whether the exercise of any guarantead right or freedom is hindered
notwithstanding the valid purpose. If it fails to pass either the purpose test
or the effects test, then an inquiry must be made to determine whether it
exceeds such reasonable limits as can be demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society.

[
13
]

There is nothing in the text of s. 121 of the
Urban Municipality Act

or of the
Store Hours Bylaw
to indicate that either was enacted as part
of a scheme to promote Sunday as a day of religious observance. Nor is there
any evidence to suggest that such was the case. Both enactments deal with the
closing hours of retail stores on all days, including Sundays, and I am
persuaded that insofar as Sunday closing is concerned their purpose is to
provide a common day away from work for retail employees. I conclude,
therefore, that both enactments have a valid purpose. But what of their
effects?

[
14
]

In
R. v. Edwards Books
there was evidence on record that those of
the Jewish and Seventh-day Adventist faiths in Ontario observe Saturday as
their Sabbath. This evidence provided a footing for the conclusion that the
Ontario statute runs foul of
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.
There is no similar
evidence in this case concerning the religious observances of those in
Saskatchewan professing the same faiths. However, I do not think that the
absence of such evidence would be a sound reason for holding that the Sunday
closing requirements of the.
Act
and the bylaw do not also run foul of
s. 2(a).

[
15
]

In Jones v.
The Queen (1987),
1986 CanLII 32 (SCC)
, 69 N.R. 241; 25 C.R.R. 63,
LaForest, J., made the following observation at page 74;

"A court must be taken to have a general knowledge of our
history and values and to know at least the broad design and workings of our
society."

It is true he was speaking in the context of an inquiry to
determine whether a certain statutory violation of the appellant's freedom of
religion could be justified. Nevertheless, I think the same observation can
apply when examining the purpose and effects of legislation in
Charter

cases. This is especially so when a court is required by
s. 27
of the
Charter

to recognize the multicultural heritage of Canadians. To me it would seem an
act of judicial blindness not to recognize that there are in the City of
Saskatoon, in the Province of Saskatchewan, persons of the Jewish and
Seventh-day Adventist faiths whose religious' day of rest is Saturday and, as
well, that some of those persons are engaged in retail trades.

[
16
]

The Ontario statute was found to impact adversely upon the freedom of
Saturday observers in that province to practice their religious beliefs. In my
opinion, the Sunday closing provisions of the
Urban Municipality Act, 1984

and the
Store Hours Bylaw
have the same impact upon Saturday observers
in Saskatchewan and thus infringe upon the freedom guaranteed by
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
.

III

[
17
]

The rights and freedoms guaranteed by the
Charter
are not without
limit.
Section 1
of the
Charter
subjects them "... to such reasonable
limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society.".

[
18
]

In
R. v. Edwards Books
, Chief Justice Dickson described at page
768 what is required to meet the test implicit in s. 1:

"Two requirements must be satisfied to establish that a
limit is reasonable and demonstrably justified in a free and democratic
society. First, the legislative objective which the limitation is designed to
promote must be of sufficient importance to warrant overriding a constitutional
right. It must bear on a 'pressing and substantial concern'. Second, the means
chosen to attain those objectives must be proportional or appropriate to the
ends. The proportionality requirement, in turn, normally has three aspects: the
limiting measures must be carefully designed, or rationally connected, to the
objective; they must impair the right as little as possible; and their effects
must not so severely trench on individual or group rights that the legislative
objective, albeit important, is nevertheless outweighed by the abridgment of
rights."

These requirements were first enunciated by the Supreme Court in
R. v. Oakes,
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103; 65 N.R. 87; 14 O.A.C. 335; 50 C.R.(3d) 1; 24
C.C.C.(3d) 321; 26 D.L.R.(4th) 200. The Ontario statute was found to have met
the test. It is unnecessary for me to reiterate the reasons given beyond saying
that the court viewed the objective of a common pause day for workers as a
matter of sufficient importance to warrant overriding a constitutional right,
and considered the limiting measures to be rationally connected to the
objective and designed to abridge the freedom of religion of Saturday observers
as little as possible. It is on the last point that a comparison of the Ontario
and Saskatchewan positions breaks down.

[
19
]

The Ontario statute contains a Sabbatarian exemption for Saturday
observing retailers. It exempts from its Sunday closing requirements those
retail stores which were closed on the previous day, provided not more than
seven people are employed in the store on Sunday and provided the store area
used on Sunday does not exceed 5000 square feet. This exemption persuaded Chief
Justice Dickson and those who concurred in his judgment that a satisfactory
legislative effort had been made to mitigate any infringement of freedom of
religion. It seems that the Chief Justice would not have found the statute to
be valid in the absence of some such exemption. At page 782 he stated:

"In my view, the principles articulated in
Oakes

make it incumbent on a legislature which enacts Sunday closing laws to attempt
very seriously to alleviate the effects of those laws on Saturday observers.
The exemption in s. 3(4) of the
Act
under review in these appeals
represents a satisfactory effort on the part of the Legislature of Ontario to
that end and is, accordingly, permissible."

Neither the Legislature of Saskatchewan nor the municipal
council of the City of Saskatoon made any attempt to alleviate the effects of
their laws on Saturday observers and that omission, it appears, is fatal.

[
20
]

In the result, I find that the Sunday closing provisions contained in
the
Urban Municipality Act, 1984
and in the
Store Hours Bylaw
do
infringe
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
and that the infringement is not
justifiable under
s. 1
.

IV

[
21
]

Section 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act
, 1982 states that any law
which is inconsistent with the provisions of the
Constitution
is, to the
extent of the inconsistency, of no force or effect. A question now arises
whether the laws which I have found to infringe
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter

are invalid in total or only of no force or effect as against those whose
freedom of religion would be infringed.

[
22
]

In

R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
, possible alternative remedial
issues were discussed. In that case, the
Lord's Day Act
was held to be
constitutionally invalid because it had no secular purpose and was directed
only at the compulsion of religious observance. However, it was recognized that
there might be cases where a person whose freedom of religion was infringed by
an otherwise valid law enacted for a secular purpose could claim a
"constitutional exemption". The matter was again broached, but left
unresolved, in
R. v. Edwards Books.

[
23
]

The present appeals involve laws enacted for a valid secular purpose but
which incidentally interfere with the religious tenets of some people. Should
those laws be regarded as invalid for all purposes or should they merely be
unenforceable as against those whose constitutional freedoms are adversely
affected? For a number of reasons I think the former to be preferable.

[
24
]

Insofar as certainty in the law is possible, it is desirable. To cast
legislation in broad terms with the understanding that it may be limited in its
application would be to promote uncertainty. For example, in the circumstances
of these appeals who would be entitled to claim a constitutional exemption?
Would an exemption be available to all Saturday observing retailers or only to
those who actually close their establishments on Saturdays for religious
reasons? Would a corporation - which cannot express a religious preference - be
denied an exemption even if all of its shareholders were Sabbatarians? This
list of uncertainties is by no means closed.

[
25
]

Also, every claim of exemption would involve an inquiry into a person's
religious beliefs, either by administrative officials, law enforcement officers
or courts, and often by all three. Official inquiries into such matters may be
demeaning and offensive and they are undesirable. Such inquiries themselves
might constitute a
Charter
violation.

[
26
]

Finally, the enforcement of a law applicable to some and not others
might encounter obstacles arising from the equality rights set out in
s. 15(1)

of the
Charter
.

[
27
]

The problem of fashioning the law to suit the
Constitution
is for
the legislators, not the courts.

[
28
]

Therefore, I conclude that the Sunday closing provisions which are the
subject of these appeals are of no force or effect.

V

[
29
]

A wider argument advanced on behalf of the respondents is that the
entire scheme of store hours regulation established by the
Act
and the
bylaw is objectionable because it collides with
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

"15.(1) Every individual is equal before and under the
law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law
without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on
race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or
physical disability."

Much of the argument concerned the meaning to be attributed to
the section. Until recently the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan had not ruled
upon the matter and there was disagreement among existing authorities. It is
unnecessary to describe the competing approaches to the problem because the
Court of Appeal has now provided some direction.

[
30
]

In the Matter of a Reference Concerning the Right of an Accused to Use
French in Criminal Proceedings in the Courts of Saskatchewan (unreported
judgment delivered July 27, 1987) [see
1987 CanLII 204 (SK CA)
, 58 Sask. R. 161], Cameron, J.A., writing
for the majority, undertook an elaborate analysis of s. 15(1). He began, at
pages 33 and 34, by referring to the preamble of the
Charter
:

"Turning first to the character and larger objects of the

Charter
itself, we note that its preamble declares that Canada is
founded upon principles that recognize, inter alia, 'the rule of law'. Among
other things, that concept embraces the notion of equality
before
the
law: that all persons, whatever their rank, birth, wealth, education, or other
condition, are equally subject to the ordinary law of the land as administered
by the ordinary courts ...

"... The rule of law, in this sense, is another
manifestation of the value, fundamental to our society, of the inherent worth
and dignity of every member of the community; .we hold to the notions that
human worth is equal and that the law must respect that equality. The purpose
of s. 15, and the interests it is meant to protect, are rooted in those
notions."

Then, at page 37:

"... we take the term 'discrimination' to have
essentially the same general meaning as that found in three human rights
treaties adopted by Canada: the
International Convention on the Elimination
of All Forms of Racial Discrimination
, 660 U.N. T.S. 195, Article 1; the
International
Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women
,
19 I L M, Article 1; and the
Convention Concerning Discrimination in Respect
of Employment and Occupation
(No. Ill), 362 U.N.T.S. 31, Article 1(a).
Picking up on the definition common to these treaties, and assuming the whole
of the section is modified by the phrase 'without discrimination', we construe
the term to mean any distinction, exclusion, restriction, or preference whose
purpose or effect is to nullify or impair the enjoyment of the forms of
equality enshrined in the section."

It is evident from these passages that the word
"discrimination" as it appears in s. 15(1) is not to be understood in
a purely pejorative sense but, at the same time, it is not every kind of
distinction or classification that is prohibited.

[
31
]

At page 47, Cameron, J.A., set out two questions which might be
appropriately posed on every s. 15(1) inquiry.

"... (i) whether, the state of affairs at issue brings
into play any of the forms of equality housed within the section, having regard
for their nature and scope, and (ii) whether, in light of the meaning we have
accorded the term 'without discrimination', the impugned measures in purpose or
effect, nullify or impair the realization of the right to that form of
equality."

Does the state of affairs at issue on these appeals bring into
play any of the forms of equality housed within the section? I think not.

[
32
]

It is said that the Act and the bylaw discriminate in at least three
ways. First, they treat retail businesses differently than other businesses.
Second, different retailers are treated differently according to the kinds of
goods they sell. Third, retailers selling similar kinds of goods are treated
differently depending on the size of their stores. All of that may be, but
those are not, in my estimation, the forms of inequality targeted by the
section.

[
33
]

The forms of equality guaranteed by s. 15(1), and the forms of
inequality forbidden, are those connected to human rights concepts of
individual worth and dignity. The regulation of businesses per se is not so
connected and is not governed by s. 15 in the absence of some trespass against
human rights objectives. I do not think the section has any application to the
circumstances presented here. Having so decided, it is unnecessary to consider
the second question set out by Mr. Justice Cameron.

VI

[
34
]

In conclusion, those appeals arising from charges of failing to close
stores on Sundays are dismissed. Those appeals arising from charges of failing
to close stores at other times are allowed, the orders of dismissal set aside,
and the charges referred back to the Provincial Court for trial.

Appeal allowed in part.
